about: The chapters alternate between a first-person narrator and a third-person account of Petra, so no single narrator may be suggested.
title: Two Lighthouses
author: Owen Hale

chapters.title: The Keeper
paragraphs: I climbed the tower at dusk, as I had every evening for eleven years. The stairs were damp and I counted them out of habit.
At the top I trimmed the wick and wiped the great lens. I could see the other light across the bay, small and steady.
I never knew who kept that light. I only knew that it was always lit a minute after mine.
The wind rose after dark. I wrote the weather in the log and drew a line under the date.
Below me the sea threw itself at the rocks. I made tea on the little stove and drank it standing by the glass.
Some nights I signalled across the bay with a hand lamp. I never once had an answer.
At midnight I wound the clockwork again. Then I sat in the chair by the window and listened to the gears.

chapters.title: Across the Bay
paragraphs: Petra lit the lamp a minute after the light across the bay, as she always did. She liked to see the other light first.
The lighthouse on her side of the bay was older and smaller. Its stairs were stone, and the rail was worn smooth by a century of hands.
Petra kept a ledger of every ship that passed. She wrote their names in a neat hand and drew a small flag beside each one.
On stormy nights she stayed awake until dawn. The lamp needed oil every three hours, and the glass needed wiping.
Sometimes a small light flickered from the other tower. Petra watched it but never answered.
In the spring a supply boat brought letters and flour. The boatman stayed for one cup of coffee and then rowed away.
Petra read the letters by the lamp. None of them were from anyone she knew well.

chapters.title: The Keeper Again
paragraphs: I saw the supply boat cross the bay in the spring. It went to the other light first and came to me last.
The boatman brought my flour and a sack of coal. I asked him who kept the other light, and he only shrugged.
That night I signalled again. I flashed the hand lamp three times and waited by the glass.
For a long time nothing happened. Then the far light flickered, once, twice, three times.
I laughed out loud in the empty tower. I signalled back until the oil in the hand lamp ran out.
In the morning I wrote it in the log. I wrote it plainly, with the time and the weather, and I underlined it twice.
